## 1. Introduction

The study of the structure of the universe is one of the most fundamental problems in physics. The large-scale structure of the universe, including galaxies, clusters of galaxies, and superclusters, has been shaped by gravitational interactions over billions of years. Understanding this structure provides insights into the initial conditions of the universe, the nature of dark matter and dark energy, and the overall evolution of cosmic structures.

One of the key tools for studying the large-scale structure of the universe is the correlation function, which quantifies the statistical relationship between the positions of galaxies or other astronomical objects. The two-point correlation function, in particular, is widely used because it captures the basic clustering properties of matter in the universe. It measures the excess probability of finding two galaxies separated by a given distance compared to what would be expected if the galaxies were distributed randomly.

In recent years, there has been significant progress in both theoretical models and observational data for understanding the large-scale structure of the universe. Advances in computational power have allowed for more detailed simulations of galaxy formation and evolution, while new surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Dark Energy Survey (DES) have provided vast amounts of data on the distribution of galaxies across the sky.

This paper aims to review the current state of knowledge regarding the large-scale structure of the universe, focusing on the two-point correlation function and its implications for cosmological parameters. We will discuss the theoretical foundations of the correlation function, its measurement from observational data, and its use in constraining cosmological models. Additionally, we will explore recent developments in the field, including the impact of baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and redshift-space distortions (RSD) on the interpretation of the correlation function.

The structure of this paper is as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the theoretical framework for the two-point correlation function. Section 3 discusses the methods used to measure the correlation function from observational data. Section 4 presents the results of recent studies and their implications for cosmological parameters. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the findings and outlines future directions for research.
